content: Weight retention following pregnancy is a contributing factor to the development of obesity. While diet and exercise are widely recognized as essential components of weight loss programs in the general population, the effectiveness of these strategies specifically for postpartum women has not been thoroughly studied. The purpose of this review was to assess the impact of dietary interventions, exercise, or a combination of both on weight reduction in postpartum women. Additionally, the review aimed to evaluate how these interventions influence maternal body composition, cardiorespiratory fitness, breastfeeding performance, and other outcomes for both the mother and child. To gather relevant data, a comprehensive search was conducted in the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register and LILACS database as of January 31, 2012. Secondary references were reviewed, and experts in the field were consulted. The search was later updated on April 30, 2013, with new findings added to the review's classification section. The review included all published and unpublished randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-randomized trials that examined the effects of diet, exercise, or both in postpartum women. Two independent reviewers assessed the quality of the trials and extracted data. Results were analyzed using risk ratios (RR) for categorical data and mean differences (MD) for continuous data. A fixed-effect model was used for analysis, with a random-effects model applied in cases of heterogeneity. A total of 14 trials were included in the review, but only 12 trials involving 910 women provided data for outcome analysis. The findings revealed that women who participated in exercise programs did not experience significantly greater weight loss compared to those in the usual care group (two trials; n = 53; MD -0.10 kg; 95% CI -1.90 to 1.71). However, women who engaged in dietary interventions (one trial; n = 45; MD -1.70 kg; 95% CI -2.08 to -1.32) or combined diet and exercise programs (seven trials; n = 573; MD -1.93 kg; 95% CI -2.96 to -0.89; random-effects, T² = 1.09, I² = 71%) achieved significantly greater weight loss compared to those receiving usual care. There was no significant difference in weight loss between the diet-alone group and the diet-plus-exercise group (one trial; n = 43; MD 0.30 kg; 95% CI -0.06 to 0.66). Importantly, the interventions did not appear to negatively impact breastfeeding performance. The authors concluded that both dietary interventions alone and in combination with exercise are effective in promoting weight loss in postpartum women. However, combining diet and exercise may be preferable, as it not only facilitates weight loss but also enhances maternal cardiorespiratory fitness and preserves fat-free mass. In contrast, diet alone may lead to a reduction in fat-free mass. These findings require further validation through large, high-quality trials. Additionally, for breastfeeding women, more evidence is needed to confirm that these interventions are safe and do not adversely affect either the mother or the infant.
